chaos_scenario.title: Simulating New Year's Eve Surge (100x Load)...

steps.label: Millions of real-time WebSocket pings absorbed
Async payment retries prevent revenue loss

levels.title: Level 1: Client Ingress & Real-Time Connections
levels.description: Establish a highly available entry point that can handle massive concurrent connections from drivers and riders.

questions.text: Millions of riders and drivers are opening the app simultaneously. What is the first infrastructure component required to route this traffic securely across healthy backend servers?
choices: A single monolithic Node.js server
An API Gateway backed by a Global Load Balancer
Direct IP routing to the database
questions.correct_answer: An API Gateway backed by a Global Load Balancer
questions.explanation: An API Gateway handles SSL termination, routing, and horizontal scaling. Paired with a load balancer, it ensures no single point of failure at the entry layer.

questions.text: Drivers send their GPS location every 3 seconds. Establishing a new HTTP connection for every ping introduces massive overhead. What protocol is better suited for this?
choices: Persistent WebSockets / Long-lived TCP connections
FTP (File Transfer Protocol)
Standard HTTP/1.1 REST calls
questions.explanation: WebSockets maintain a persistent, bi-directional connection, drastically reducing hand-shake overhead and latency for high-frequency location streaming.

questions.text: Malicious bots occasionally flood the entry point attempting to scrape pricing data or exhaust resources. How do we protect the backend?
choices: Web Application Firewall (WAF) & Rate Limiter at the API Gateway
Manually blocking IPs in the database
Closing the WebSocket connections randomly
questions.correct_answer: Web Application Firewall (WAF) & Rate Limiter at the API Gateway
questions.explanation: A WAF and rate limiter intercept bad traffic at the edge, protecting expensive downstream compute resources from DDoS attacks and abuse.
questions.uml_mutation:
api --> waf[WAF & Rate Limiter]
    waf --> ws

levels.title: Level 2: Location Tracking & Matchmaking
levels.description: Ingest high-throughput data streams and architect fast spatial querying for dispatching.

questions.text: The WebSocket cluster receives millions of GPS pings per second. If we write these directly to a database, it will crash. How do we buffer this write-heavy workload?
choices: Write them to local text files on the WebSocket servers
Use a high-throughput message queue like Apache Kafka
Pause driver connections until the database catches up
questions.correct_answer: Use a high-throughput message queue like Apache Kafka
questions.explanation: Kafka acts as a shock absorber. It durably ingests millions of events per second and decouples the ingestion layer from the workers processing the locations.

questions.text: To dispatch a ride, the system must instantly find all drivers within a 2-mile radius. Which storage technology and indexing strategy provides the lowest latency for this?
choices: An in-memory Geospatial index (e.g., Redis Geo / QuadTree / H3)
A standard relational table doing full-table scans
HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System)
questions.correct_answer: An in-memory Geospatial index (e.g., Redis Geo / QuadTree / H3)
questions.explanation: In-memory geospatial databases divide the world into spatial grids (like Geohashes or H3), allowing O(1) or O(log N) lookups for nearby drivers instead of scanning all users.
questions.uml_mutation:
kafka --> locSvc[Location Service]
    locSvc --> redis[(Redis Geospatial)]

questions.text: Now that we know where drivers are, a rider requests a trip. Which microservice coordinates querying the Location Service and pushing the offer to the best driver?
choices: The Matchmaking / Dispatch Service
The API Gateway itself
The Driver's mobile phone
questions.explanation: A dedicated Dispatch Service contains the complex business logic to evaluate ETA, driver scores, and route the ride offer to the most optimal candidate via the WebSocket connection.
questions.uml_mutation:
api --> dispatch[Dispatch Service]
    dispatch --> locSvc
    dispatch -.->|Offer Ride| ws

levels.title: Level 3: Trip Management & Data Persistence
levels.description: Manage long-running state machines and persist data accurately across different database paradigms.

questions.text: Once a driver accepts, the ride moves through states (Arrived, In Transit, Completed). Which service is responsible for this state machine?
choices: Trip Management Service
Location Service
Global Load Balancer
questions.explanation: The Trip Management Service orchestrates the lifecycle of a ride, acting as the source of truth for the current state of any active booking.

questions.text: Completed trips generate massive amounts of historical data, which is mostly queried by Trip ID or User ID. What database paradigm fits this high-write, horizontally scalable workload?
choices: A single monolithic SQLite file
A distributed NoSQL database (e.g., Cassandra / DynamoDB)
A Redis Cache with an eviction policy
questions.correct_answer: A distributed NoSQL database (e.g., Cassandra / DynamoDB)
questions.explanation: Wide-column or Key-Value NoSQL databases like Cassandra are optimized for massive write throughput and allow seamless horizontal scaling by partitioning data across many nodes.

questions.text: When the trip ends, the user's credit card is charged. Payment data requires strict ACID compliance (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). What database is best?
choices: A Relational SQL Database (e.g., PostgreSQL / MySQL)
A graph database like Neo4j
Kafka Event Stream
questions.correct_answer: A Relational SQL Database (e.g., PostgreSQL / MySQL)
questions.explanation: Relational databases provide strict ACID guarantees, which are legally and financially required to ensure no double-charges or lost financial transactions.
questions.uml_mutation:
tripSvc --> paySvc[Payment Service]
    paySvc --> pgsql[(Payment DB / PostgreSQL)]

levels.title: Level 4: Streaming Analytics & Resilience
levels.description: Implement dynamic surge pricing, handle external failures gracefully, and monitor system health.

questions.text: To calculate Surge Pricing, we need to analyze supply (driver pings) and demand (app opens) in real-time. How should we process this data?
choices: Run a nightly batch job on the database
Use a Stream Processing Engine (e.g., Apache Flink / Spark Streaming) reading from Kafka
Have the Dispatch Service calculate it synchronously on every request
questions.correct_answer: Use a Stream Processing Engine (e.g., Apache Flink / Spark Streaming) reading from Kafka
questions.explanation: Stream processing engines consume events from Kafka in real-time, compute aggregations (like demand heatmaps) over sliding time windows, and update surge multipliers instantly.
questions.uml_mutation:
kafka --> flink[Stream Processing (Flink)]
    flink --> pricing[Surge Pricing Service]
    dispatch --> pricing

questions.text: External payment gateways (like Stripe) sometimes go down. How do we ensure we don't lose the payment data if the charge fails due to a network error?
choices: Show the driver an error and tell them they won't be paid
Use an async Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) to retry failed payments with exponential backoff
Restart the Trip Management Service
questions.correct_answer: Use an async Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) to retry failed payments with exponential backoff
questions.explanation: A Retry Queue/DLQ durably stores failed tasks. Workers can retry processing the payment later when the third-party gateway recovers, ensuring eventual consistency.
questions.uml_mutation:
paySvc --> dlq[[Retry & DLQ Kafka]]
    dlq -.->|Backoff Retry| paySvc

questions.text: During a New Year's Eve surge, you need to track how long a request takes jumping from the API, to Dispatch, to Trip Service. What infrastructure solves this?
choices: Distributed Tracing (e.g., Jaeger / OpenTelemetry)
Printing the time to standard output (stdout)
Using ping commands in the terminal
questions.explanation: Distributed tracing attaches a unique Correlation ID to the request at the gateway, tracing its path and latency across all microservices to pinpoint bottlenecks.
questions.uml_mutation:
api --> obs[Observability Platform]
    dispatch --> obs
    tripSvc --> obs
    style kafka fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399
    style redis fill:#065f46,stroke:#34d399
